notes.meaning: The people listening in the crowd interrupted Jesus because they were surprised by the master's decision. They pointed out that the faithful servant already had ten pounds, so giving him one more seemed unfair. They did not yet understand the spiritual lesson Jesus was teaching about faithful service.

Jesus explains a basic rule of God's kingdom: whoever faithfully uses what they are given will receive even more. Anyone who does nothing with what God gave them will end up losing even the little they had. Diligence in serving God brings greater opportunities, while neglect leads to spiritual loss.

The king commands that the rebellious citizens who refused his rule be brought forward and put to death in his presence. This foretold the destruction that would fall upon Jerusalem for rejecting Jesus, as well as the final judgment of all who reject His royal authority. Those who will not submit to Christ as their King will ultimately face His judgment.

differ.view: Calvin noted that this warning applied mainly to the Jewish nation, but it was also spoken to comfort and strengthen believers to remain faithful during troubled times.

notes.meaning: After telling this parable, Jesus walked on ahead of His disciples toward Jerusalem. He knew the suffering and death waiting for Him there, yet He led the way boldly and willingly. He was not forced to go to the cross; He went ahead of them all to finish His work.

As Jesus drew near the villages of Bethphage and Bethany on the Mount of Olives, He sent two of His disciples ahead. This location fulfilled ancient prophecies about where the Messiah would appear. Jesus carefully directed every step of His arrival in the holy city.

Jesus told the two disciples to enter the village ahead and untie a young donkey that had never been ridden. An animal that had never carried a burden was set apart for a sacred, royal purpose. They were commanded to untie it and bring it straight to Jesus.

Jesus gave the disciples the exact words to say if anyone asked why they were taking the animal: 'The Lord needs it.' He showed that He possessed supreme authority over all creation and knew the hearts of men. He knew the owners would willingly agree once they heard that message.

The two disciples went into the village and found everything just as Jesus had told them. His exact knowledge of where the colt was proved His divine power and foresight. Their simple obedience was met with complete success.

As the disciples were untying the young donkey, its owners saw them and asked what they were doing. The owners had every right to protect their property and question strangers. This gave the disciples the opportunity to deliver the message Jesus had given them.

The disciples answered with the words Jesus had given them: 'The Lord needs it.' Hearing this, the owners were completely satisfied and allowed them to take the colt away without an argument. God moved their hearts to gladly supply what Jesus needed.

The disciples brought the young donkey to Jesus, threw their outer coats across its back to serve as a saddle, and helped Him mount. Riding a donkey fulfilled prophecy and showed He was a peaceful King, not a military conqueror on a warhorse. His followers gladly gave up their own clothes to honor Him.

As Jesus rode along, people spread their cloaks on the dirt road ahead of Him. In Bible times, laying garments in someone's path was a traditional way to show honor and loyalty to a king. The crowd showed their readiness to welcome Jesus as their royal leader.

When Jesus reached the downhill path from the Mount of Olives, the large crowd of disciples joyfully praised God in loud voices. They had seen many powerful miracles, especially Jesus raising Lazarus from the dead, and could no longer hold back their excitement. Seeing the holy city before them stirred their hope that the Messiah had finally come.

The crowd shouted royal blessings from Scripture, declaring Jesus to be the blessed King who comes in the name and authority of the Lord. They proclaimed peace in heaven and the highest glory to God. Their joyful words echoed the song the angels sang when Jesus was born.

other.label: Orthodox
other.view: Orthodox teaching observes that while the crowd rightly praised Jesus as King, many misunderstood Him as an earthly political leader, and Christians are warned not to be like those who praised Him on Palm Sunday but soon demanded His death.

notes.meaning: Some Pharisees in the crowd were outraged by this public praise and told Jesus to silence His followers. They did not believe He was the Messiah and thought giving Him such high honor was wrong. They may also have feared that treating Jesus as a king would provoke the Roman authorities.

Jesus replied that if the disciples kept silent, the very stones along the road would cry out in praise. His arrival as the promised Messiah was such a momentous event that God's glory could not be contained. Even if men refused to praise Him, creation itself would declare His royal dignity.

differ.view: Wesley explained that if people held their peace, God would raise up the most unlikely and unexpected instruments to proclaim His praise.
Godbey saw Jesus' words as a full defense of loud, joyful expressions in worship, much like the shouting found at holiness camp meetings.

notes.meaning: As Jesus drew close enough to see Jerusalem clearly, He burst into loud weeping over the city. Even while the crowds around Him were rejoicing, His heart was broken by the coming tragedy He foresaw. His tears proved His deep, tender compassion for people who were heading toward ruin.

differ.view: Calvin taught that Jesus wept out of real human love as Mediator and teacher, while His divine power remained quietly hidden so He could truly feel and grieve for the lost.
Bengel observed that while Jesus wept deeply over the city and longed to save it, He would not force anyone to believe against their will.

notes.meaning: Jesus broke off His words in deep sorrow, wishing that the city had recognized what would bring them true peace with God. Instead, they had rejected the light and salvation offered to them. Because they chose to turn away from God, the truth was now hidden from their eyes as a judgment.

Jesus warned of a coming day when enemies would build dirt walls around Jerusalem to trap everyone inside. This prophecy came true about forty years later when the Roman general Titus besieged the city. The Roman soldiers built a wall encircling the entire city in just days, cutting off all food and escape.

Jesus warned that the invaders would completely flatten the city, destroy the people within its walls, and not leave one stone standing upon another. This terrible disaster fell on Jerusalem because they failed to recognize the time when God visited them in the person of His Son. The Roman armies later destroyed the city and the temple just as Jesus said.

When Jesus entered Jerusalem, He went straight into the temple and began driving out the merchants who were buying and selling there. This was the second time He cleansed the temple, showing His divine authority over His Father's house at the very end of His ministry. He showed that sacred places must be kept pure for God rather than used for worldly profit.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Ambrose taught that the merchants represent people who misuse Scripture for personal gain, and that the temple also pictures the soul of a believer, which must be cleansed from sin.

notes.meaning: Jesus quoted the Old Testament to remind them that God's house is meant to be a place of prayer and communion with God. Instead, dishonest sellers had turned it into a hideout for thieves by cheating worshippers through unfair business practices. Jesus defended the honor of God's sanctuary and called the people back to sincere worship.

Jesus spent the remaining days before the Passover teaching in the temple courtyards every day. At the same time, the chief priests, scribes, and leading men of the nation were actively plotting to murder Him. Instead of listening to God's Son, the nation's spiritual leaders were bent on destroying Him.

The religious leaders could not find a way to harm Jesus because the common people hung on every word He spoke. The crowd listened with intense interest and would not leave His side, which kept the leaders from arresting Him. The people's deep attention protected Jesus until His appointed hour arrived.
